desc.en: ¬a: true in gives false out; false in gives true out.
a ∧ b: outputs true only when both inputs are true; otherwise false.
From A → B and A, gives B.
From A → B and A, gives B. ¬A is A → ⊥, so from ¬A and A, gives the contradiction ⊥.
A box, with A set on the part. Inside, A may be used as an assumption; prove B there and wire it to “Conclusion”, and the part gives A → B.
Connect A and B to get A ∧ B.
Connect A ∧ B to get A and B at separate outputs.
Connect A ∧ B to get A and B at separate outputs. A ↔ B means (A → B) ∧ (B → A) and can be split in the same way.
Connect A and choose another statement B and its position to get A ∨ B or B ∨ A. B need not be proved.
Connect A ∨ B and assume A and B in separate boxes. When both prove the same C and connect it to their respective “Conclusion” ports, the part outputs C.
From the contradiction ⊥, gives whatever sentence is chosen on the part.
From ¬¬A, gives A (double-negation elimination).
Name an arbitrary object a on the part. Prove P(a) inside the box and connect it to “Conclusion” to obtain ∀x. P(x) outside. a must not occur in any open assumption.
Connect ∀x. P(x) and choose an object t to obtain P(t).
Connect P(t) to obtain ∃x. P(x), with t as a witness. If exactly one existential statement fits, it is selected automatically; if several fit, choose the conclusion on the part.

Connect ∃x. P(x) and name the existing object a on the part. Inside the box, P(a) may be assumed. Prove C and connect it to “Conclusion” to obtain C outside. a must not appear in C or in any open assumption.

Two boxes, proving the ∀x. P(x) chosen on the part. The first proves P(0); in the second the number is called a (named on the part; it must not occur in any open assumption), P(a) may be used as an assumption, and P(S a) is to be proved. Once both are proved, the part gives ∀x. P(x).
Choose a thing t on the part; gives t = t.
Wire in s = t and a sentence containing s; the part marks each s in it, and the ticked ones become t.
Gives ?R: any sentence at all.
Wire in a rule and a sentence: keeps the rule’s premises and makes the sentence its conclusion.
Puts “This” at the front of “A list”; when what comes into “A list” is not a list, makes a list of the two.
Builds the rule ⟦premises⟧ ⟹ conclusion from premises (a list or a single item) and a conclusion. A sentence is a premise as it is; a rule becomes a premise with its own assumptions.
Wire in a list: the frame receives one item at a time, and its inner output goes to “Result”; each item is processed once, and the results form a list in the original order.

Wire in a rule. If it begins with bound variables (⋀x. …), the frame works on the rule after them, and the output keeps the same bound variables in front; if it has none, the frame works on the input itself.

label.en: The rule after the bound variables

desc.en: Finds an equation with identical sides, t ≐ t, and deletes it.

Finds an equation whose sides have the same structure (both “and”, the same predicate …) and splits it into equations between corresponding parts: ?A ∧ ?B ≐ it rains ∧ it is windy becomes ?A ≐ it rains and ?B ≐ it is windy. ¬A splits as A → ⊥.

Finds an equation whose sides have the same structure and splits it into equations between corresponding parts. When both sides are “for all” (or both “there is”), it takes out the two bodies with one variable x for both, and marks the equation ⋀x: x is bound by a quantifier.
Finds an equation with no ?-letter on either side and different structures (an “and” against an “or”, two different sentences …) and reports failure.
Finds an equation with a ?-letter on the right only, t ≐ ?A, and turns it into ?A ≐ t.
Finds ?A ≐ t where t contains ?A and is not ?A itself, and reports failure.
Finds ?A ≐ t where ?A cannot be t and reports failure: t contains ?A and is not ?A itself, or t contains a variable bound by the ⋀ in front.
Finds ?A ≐ t (t free of ?A) where ?A still occurs in other equations, and replaces ?A with t there.

Finds ⋀x. ?P(x) ≐ t where ?P is applied to distinct variables bound by the ⋀ and t contains no other ⋀ variable, and solves ?P ≐ fun x => t. When ?P is applied to anything else (?P(ann), ?P(?t)), the equation is left unchanged.

The frame receives the input; its inner output goes to “Result” and back into the frame, round after round, until it stops changing, and the last round’s result is given. If a round fails, it stops at the round before.

The frame receives the input; its inner output goes to “Result” and back into the frame, round after round, until it stops changing, and the last round’s result is given. If a round fails, it stops at the round before. With several results, it goes on from the first only.

Takes rules at its “Rules” port and uses the first that applies: the first goal is unified with the rule’s conclusion and replaced by its premises (one goal per premise, each premise’s own assumptions added to the hypotheses). Any ?-letter not yet fixed stays in the goals.
Unifies the first goal with one of its hypotheses: on success the goal is closed and its ?-letters are fixed. It searches from the top and uses the first that fits.
Unifies the first goal with one of its hypotheses: on success that goal is closed. Each hypothesis that fits gives one result, in order from the top.
Moves the first goal to the end; the second becomes the first.
Every region receives the same state; gives the result of the first region that does not fail. The number of regions is chosen on the part.
Every region receives the same state; gives every result of the first region, then every result of the next, and so on; a region that fails gives none. The number of regions is chosen on the part.

Depth-first search: the parts inside take one step on the state received, then go on from each result; each path is followed to its end before backtracking to the next, until no goal remains. Gives every finished state it finds. A step back to where it was (no fewer goals, no more hypotheses) is not followed. A depth limit can be set on the part.
The parts inside run once on each goal, seeing only that goal each time; if any goal fails, the whole part fails.

Takes rewrite rules: in the first goal, outside in and left to right, the first place that fits the rule’s left side becomes its right side, that place alone. A rule with conditions adds each as a new goal after this one. Given several, it uses the first that fits; if nothing fits, it fails.

Takes rewrite rules: in the first goal, outside in and left to right, the first place that fits the rule’s left side becomes its right side, that place alone. A rule with conditions adds each as a new goal after this one. Given several, it uses the first that fits; if nothing fits, it fails. With “Where” set to the hypotheses, it rewrites the first goal’s first hypothesis from the top that fits.

Removes every ∃ from the first goal’s hypotheses: one with no ∀ outside is taken out as the instance box does; one under a ∀ becomes a new function of all the enclosing ∀ variables (sk1(x) …). The hypotheses must be in negation normal form first.

The first goal must be ⊥: its hypotheses are split into clauses. Each must be in CNF; conjunctions are split, each disjunction becomes a clause, ∀s are dropped and variables read as universally quantified.

Tries every pair of clauses in the set once: when a literal of one unifies with the complement of a literal of the other, that pair is cancelled and the remaining literals form a new clause, added with a record of its two parents. Tautologies and duplicates are dropped. It can be set to resolve only against one-literal clauses.
A fast prover: it cancels all complementary literals between two clauses at once, round after round until ⊥ appears or no new clause does. It too records the two parents of each new clause.

When the clause set contains ⊥, the steps to ⊥ go to the kernel: each input clause used must come from a hypothesis, and each step must be proved from its two parents (variables instantiated by unification) by Own auto. If all pass, the goal the clauses came from is proved; otherwise it names the failing step.
Outputs true when at least one input is true; false when both are false.
Outputs false only when a is true and b is false; true otherwise.
a ↔ b: outputs true when a and b are both true or both false; false when one is true and the other false.
Choose two sentences A and B on the part; gives A → (B → A).
Choose three sentences A, B and C on the part; gives (A → (B → C)) → ((A → B) → (A → C)).
From A → B and B → C, gives A → C.
From A → (B → C), gives B → (A → C).
From A → (A → B), gives A → B.
A negation trades “or” for “and” and back, four shapes switched on the part: ¬(A ∨ B) and ¬A ∧ ¬B give each other, and so do ¬(A ∧ B) and ¬A ∨ ¬B.
A negation trades “or” for “and”, “there is” for “for all”, and back: eight shapes switched on the part.
Two shapes switched on the part: from ¬¬A, gives A; from A, gives ¬¬A.
Two shapes switched on the part: from ¬¬A, gives A; from A, gives ¬¬A. Each shape is also a rewrite rule.
Two shapes switched on the part: from A → B, gives ¬A ∨ B; from ¬A ∨ B, gives A → B.
Two shapes switched on the part: from A → B, gives ¬A ∨ B; from ¬A ∨ B, gives A → B. Each shape is also a rewrite rule.
“Or” distributed over “and”, four shapes switched on the part: A ∨ (B ∧ C) and (A ∨ B) ∧ (A ∨ C) give each other, and so do (A ∧ B) ∨ C and (A ∨ C) ∧ (B ∨ C).
“Or” distributed over “and”, four shapes switched on the part: A ∨ (B ∧ C) and (A ∨ B) ∧ (A ∨ C) give each other, and so do (A ∧ B) ∨ C and (A ∨ C) ∧ (B ∨ C). Each shape is also a rewrite rule.
Two shapes switched on the part: from A ↔ B, gives (¬A ∨ B) ∧ (¬B ∨ A), and the other way round. Each shape is also a rewrite rule.
Wire in two clauses, one holding A and the other ¬A, in any position: that pair is cancelled and what is left is joined with “or”; when nothing is left, gives the contradiction ⊥. One pair at a time.
From A ↔ ¬A, gives the contradiction ⊥.
Choose a sentence A on the part; gives A ∨ ¬A.
Wire in a declaration (the declared sentence and its list of introduction rules); gives the declaration’s elimination rule.
Solves a set of equations to the end: each with a ?-letter on the left and none of those letters on any right side (the most general unifier); reports failure if there is none.

Solves a set of equations to the end: each with a ?-letter on the left and none of those letters on any right side (the most general unifier); reports failure if there is none. An equation like ?P(x) is not solved but left as it is.

Takes rules: the rule’s conclusion is unified with the first goal and its first premise with one of that goal’s hypotheses; the goal is replaced by the remaining premises, one goal each. Given several rules, it uses the first that applies.

Takes rules: the rule’s conclusion is unified with the first goal and its first premise with one of that goal’s hypotheses; the goal is replaced by the remaining premises, one goal each. Each rule wired in, and each hypothesis that fits, gives one result.

Takes rules: the rule’s first premise is unified with one of the first goal’s hypotheses and its conclusion is added to the hypotheses; each remaining premise becomes a goal, placed first. Given several rules, it uses the first that applies.
Applies every introduction rule backwards to the first goal: Join, the assumption box, Add alternative left and right, the for-any box, Generalise. Each rule that fits gives one result.
Applies every elimination rule to the hypotheses: Split, Case analysis, applying an “if”, Explosion, the instance box, and choose an instance then use it. Each fit gives one result.
Searches depth first until done: each step tries Assumption, then Goal apart, then Use a given; a path back to an earlier state is not followed.
Takes a list of rewrite rules: each round, the first that fits rewrites one place, round after round, until none fits.
Takes a list of rewrite rules: each round, the first that fits rewrites one place, round after round, until none fits. With “Where” set to the hypotheses, it rewrites the first goal’s hypotheses.
Adds the negated goal to the hypotheses, brings them to CNF, removes the ∃s and splits them into clauses.
Resolves round after round until ⊥ appears or no new clause does.
Turns the goal into clauses, finds a certificate that reaches ⊥ and has the kernel replay it: if it passes, the goal is closed; if the certificate fails the check, the part fails.
x + 0 = x: a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
x + S y = S (x + y): a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
x + y = y + x: a rule, and a rewrite rule; in Simp it rewrites back and forth without end.
(x + y) + z = x + (y + z): a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
xs ++ [] = xs: a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
(xs ++ ys) ++ zs = xs ++ (ys ++ zs): a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
rev (xs ++ ys) = rev ys ++ rev xs: a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
S x = S y → x = y, as a rule that takes apart: when S ?x = S ?y is given, the proof goes on from ?x = ?y instead.
u = true → (if u then v else w) = v: a rule, and a rewrite rule with a condition.
u = false → (if u then v else w) = w: a rule, and a rewrite rule with a condition.
x ≠ S x: a rule.
len (ins x xs) = S (len xs): a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
